Here's why most innovations fail and why yours doesn't have to. 75 % Venture-Backed Failure Of venture-backed startups never return cash to investors. Funding is not traction. Most never find a market that pays. Harvard Business School (Shikhar Ghosh) ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We structure every engagement around validated bets. Fail fast and cheap before you bet big. 80 % AI Projects Fail Of AI projects fail, roughly twice the failure rate of conventional IT projects. The bottleneck is rarely the model. RAND Corporation (2024) ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We ship AI that earns its keep. Scoped to a real job, measured against a baseline, killed if it doesn't beat it. 80 % 03 Feature Bloat Of features in the average product are rarely or never used. Innovation isn't doing more. It's solving the right problem well. Pendo, Feature Adoption Report ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We run Jobs-to-be-Done workshops to find the 20% worth building. The rest is noise. 70 % 04 Transformations Fail Of business transformations fail to meet their objectives. They stall on people and execution, not technology. McKinsey & Company ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We build milestone accountability into every sprint. No bailing without data behind the call. 43 % 05 No Product-Market Fit Of failed startups never found product-market fit. They built something nobody needed badly enough to pay for. CB Insights, Why Startups Fail ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS PMF is the start, not the finish line. We design the business model alongside the product from day one. Show all facts (+4) Show fewer facts 29 % 06 Bad Timing Of startup failures are pinned on bad timing or market conditions. Too early is as fatal as too late. CB Insights, Why Startups Fail ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We validate timing before you commit resources. Customer readiness is testable, so we test it. 42 % 07 Abandoned AI Of companies scrapped most of their AI initiatives in 2025, up from 17% a year earlier. Pilots rarely survive contact with production. S&P Global Market Intelligence, via CIO Dive (2025) ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We design for production from day one, not a demo. If it can't ship, we don't start it. 56 % 08 Cost & Value Gap Large IT projects deliver 56% less value than predicted, while running 45% over budget. Scope grows, value doesn't. McKinsey & University of Oxford ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS We scope honestly. No low-balling to win the deal and upsell later. 74 % 09 Premature Scaling Of high-growth startups that failed did so from premature scaling, growing faster than product or market could bear. Startup Genome (Premature Scaling report) ↗ HOW WE FIX THIS Smallest viable bet, fastest feedback loop. We help you scale when the data says go, not before. 10 × On average, a new product needs to be perceived 10x better before customers will bother switching. No Bullshit FAQ The questions everyone asks. Answered straight. Still have a question? Get in touch 01 I've been burned by an agency before. What's different here? Three structural differences. No billable hours, we sell outcomes, not timesheets. Cancel any week, no exit fees, no notice period, no scope-creep contract trap. Founder-led delivery, the people in the diagnostic call are the people writing the code, not account managers handing you off to juniors. The reason most agency relationships go bad is incentive misalignment. Ours is structured against that on purpose. 02 Why should I trust you over hiring in-house? You shouldn't, eventually. We're the gap before you can. When the senior engineer you'd hire is 4+ months away and you have 8 weeks of runway pressure, we're the bridge. We aim to put ourselves out of a job. When you can hire your CTO, we hand over a documented codebase and walk. Customers have done this. We're proud of it, not threatened by it. 03 What's the catch with 'cancel any week, refund the last week'? The catch is on us. Every week we don't earn the next one is a loss. The clause is real, and we don't plan to let that happen. The structural alternative (long retainers, exit fees, 'managed services contracts') locks in revenue regardless of outcome. We chose the opposite. If we're not blowing you away, you stop paying. That's why it works. 04 Two founders shipping mission-critical software. What's the bus factor? Team is bigger than two. Every project is documented, version-controlled, and built on standard frameworks. No bespoke proprietary stack. Knowledge transfer is built into the engagement, your team can read, run, and modify everything we ship. We've handed off cleanly to internal teams more than a dozen times. The bus factor is 'your codebase keeps working', not 'Kevin and Chris stay alive'. 05 How visible is the work? I'm scared of agencies hiding bad news. You get our Linear board, weekly sprint demos with a working build, and direct Slack/Discord access to the engineers doing the work, not a layer of account managers. You see bugs the same day we see them. You see the deploys. You see the customer-interview notes. The model is 'you're a teammate', not 'you're a client we report to once a month'. 06 What does it cost? Two engagement models. Weekly retainers: Fractional Co-Founder €400/wk, Software QA €750/wk, full-team development retainer €10–30k/mo. Cancel any week. Not happy with last week? Refunded. Fixed-price projects: €3,500 Discovery scopes everything, then a fixed quote split into milestones. The €3,500 comes off the final invoice. Either way, no hour-tracking, no scope-creep billing. 07 How long does a project take? Depends on what 'done' means for you. A prototype: days to a week. A validated MVP with paying users: 6–12 weeks. Production-ready software at scale: longer, and we'll tell you the real number after Discovery, not the number you want to hear. We're AI-native, which accelerates build speed by 30–50%. We don't skip QA and testing phases. We'd rather ship something solid than ship fast and break things. 08 What if I only have an idea and no specs? That's exactly what our Fractional Co-Founder lane is for. We validate demand with you before you spend money on the wrong build. If you've already vibe-coded a rough prototype, even better. That's the fastest way to align on direction. Specs are an output, not a prerequisite. 09 How does The No-Bullshit Guarantee work? Three rules, no fine print. (1) Cancel any week: no notice period, no exit fee, no questions. (2) Refund the last week if we didn't blow you away. You ask, you get it. (3) No hours tracked. We work to exceed expectations, not to fill timesheets. All three are written into your retainer contract. Contractual terms, not marketing claims. Refunds apply to the most recent week and cover all weekly retainers. Fixed-price projects deliver against a signed statement of work, a different but equally honest mechanism. And yes, if expectations are detached from reality, we walk too. But walking out is not walking away. You get a documented codebase, a working build, and a clean handover, every time. No client is left mid-build with broken software. That's why this works. About Company ▾ About How Wavect Evolved Expert Network Ernesto About Proof ▾ Industries Clients Testimonials Press About Evaluate us ▾ Compare Enterprise Trust Center Contact WHO RUNS WAVECT Founded by engineers tired of agency theatre . Two founders. A vetted network. No account managers, no handoffs, no slide decks. The people who write the email are the people writing the code. Kevin Riedl 01/02 Christof Jori 02/02 2018 Founded in Tyrol 75+ Products shipped 18+ Countries with clients 15 min Reply during work hours ORIGIN We started Wavect because the agency model is broken. We'd both spent years inside agencies, consultancies, and venture-backed startups before founding Wavect in 2018. We'd seen the same pattern repeat: the engineers who diagnosed the problem on the discovery call were not the engineers writing the code six weeks later. The senior who closed the deal got reassigned to the next pitch. The juniors inherited the work, lost the context, and shipped something the client never asked for. So we built the opposite. At least one of us is on every call, on every commit, on every deploy. We have no salespeople, no account managers, no project managers in the middle. If you book a call with Wavect, you book a call with the person who will write the code, or who will tell you honestly that we're the wrong team for it. We used to be a bigger team. We shrank on purpose. Headcount used to be the thing you bought when you needed more output, and for most of software's history that held: more features meant more engineers. That equation broke. We ship more, faster, with fewer people than the version of Wavect that carried a bigger payroll, and we stopped pretending the old math still works. Here is the bet we're running. The constraint in software is no longer how many engineers you can hire. It's focus, tooling, process, and the energy bill behind the models. We build AI-native: small senior teams that drive frontier models for the hard reasoning and run local models where data can't leave the building, instead of throwing bodies at the problem. A heavy team is now a liability, not a moat. It slows the feedback loop, dilutes accountability, and spends budget on coordination instead of output. Staying small is not something we apologise for. It's the whole strategy. The pricing followed from the structure. We don't bill hours, because hours are a metric for filling timesheets, not for shipping outcomes. We invoice weekly. You cancel any week. If the last week didn't blow you away, you tell us, and we refund it. The deal is structurally aligned: every week, we have to earn the next one. Fixed prices are on the table too, but in the AI age our experience is that retainers consistently get you better results: tighter feedback cycles, higher velocity, and the freedom to redirect scope the moment the work makes the next call obvious. What we do has also widened since then. We came up Web3-native and still ship blockchain, and today do just as much AI, fractional leadership and full-stack software. The fuller story: how Wavect evolved . We also have one colleague who ignores every org chart: meet Ernesto, Wavect's sarcastic company mascot . HOW WE WORK Four operating principles Outcomes, not hours. We sell ship-dates and ship-quality, not timesheets. If we're optimising for billable hours, we're not optimising for your product. Founder-led delivery. The two of us are on every project. No account managers, no junior-on-junior handoffs. Knowledge transfer is built into the engagement, not bolted on at exit. Honest 'no'. When a project would be a bad fit (scope, stack, stage, or budget), we say so on the first call and point you somewhere honest. Saying no is a service. Document everything. Every project ships with running documentation. We hand off cleanly. You should be able to fire us at any time and your codebase keeps working. THE TWO PEOPLE The people writing the code No account managers in the middle. The names on the invoice are the names on the commits. Kevin Riedl Managing Director · Operations & Product Tyrol, Austria Kevin founded Wavect in 2018. His side of the business is product, scope, and the customer call: the discovery work that decides whether a feature is worth building before any code gets written. He came up as an engineer, though. Coding since 13, still in the pull requests, across TypeScript, C# and Rust, and the FinTech-grade systems where a rounding error is a lawsuit. Product instincts forged across 75+ shipped products at Wavect, usually the hard way: in production, with real users. The job is making sure your product actually gets used. Read full bio LinkedIn GitHub Christof Jori Managing Director · Software Vienna, Austria Christof joined Wavect in 2022 and runs the technical side of every engagement: architecture, code review, the call where a stack decision gets locked in, the production deploy. A senior backend engineer whose specialty is the quiet half of the craft: test-driven development, QA, and the system reliability that keeps enterprise software standing when the load arrives. It has, for LivLive, Twinsoft AI, and ~40 others. Read full bio LinkedIn GitHub BEYOND THE TWO Backed by a vetted network of 15+ specialists Two people don't cover every domain. For specialist depth, we pull from a network we've shipped with. Not LinkedIn intros, not marketplaces. How we vet Shipped with us first. Every specialist worked a paid engagement under our review before going on yours. No first-time bets at your expense. Reference-checked with prior clients. If we wouldn't hire them ourselves, we don't bring them to you. Senior floor: 8+ years post-grad in their domain, with production work we've personally reviewed. Not a CV claim. Paid trial on a real slice of the project before they touch a critical path. Drops out fast if the work doesn't hold. When we pull a specialist in Failure mode is irreversible. Security, financial, regulatory. Bugs that can't be patched after launch. Spotting the failure mode takes 5+ years. ZK proofs, LLM evals, audit-grade cryptography, hardware/firmware, anywhere the wrong answer looks right at first glance. The architecture decision locks you in for 18+ months. Worth a second pair of senior eyes before the bet gets made. One contract, one accountable team. Specialists invoice through us. If their work breaks, we own the fix. Meet the network → Brought in. Not introduced. When a brief needs depth our bench doesn't carry, the specialist plugs into the Wavect SoW. One contract. We stay on the hook. WHERE Run from a village in the Austrian Alps. Wavect GmbH is registered in Ampass, Tirol , a 1,500-person mountain village six minutes east of Innsbruck. We're remote-first with most clients (Austria, Germany, Switzerland, the UK, the US, Singapore, the UAE), but we keep a physical office here for the same reason most decent things still happen offline: deep work needs walls, and our part of Austria has the kind of quiet that makes complicated software possible. No matter where you are: we've made it work before, Australia to West-Coast US. Read more → Manuel Licha Original Independently rated 5.0/5 on Clutch Read the reviews → Verified on Clutch · 2026 Top Digital Transformation Company in Austria View our Clutch profile → × FAQs Common questions about our Fractional Co-Founder program How does the weekly cancellation actually work? + End any week, with one message. No notice period, no exit interview, no fine print. We invoice weekly, so the most you’re ever committed to is the current week. What if I'm not blown away by the work? + It’s in your contract: tell us, and we refund that week. No questions, no invoices to dispute, no calls to escalate. The only rule: refunds apply to the most recent week. Why don't you track hours? + Because hours are the wrong metric. If we optimize for hours billed, we do not optimize for your outcome. The deal is simpler: every week has a defined result, and we earn the next week by delivering it. You pay for progress against that result, not for a timesheet. What does 'expectations detached from reality' mean? + We work with operators, not lottery winners. If a request would require breaking physics, the law, or a third party’s systems, we say so, and if we can’t align, we walk. The guarantee is mutual: you can fire us any week; we can also fire ourselves. How is this different from hiring a product consultant or business analyst? + Consultants give recommendations and leave. Business analysts document requirements. We become deeply invested in your product’s success and work hands-on to validate, iterate, and define your roadmap. We don’t just analyze, we experiment, test assumptions, and prepare everything needed for successful development. Think of us as your product co-founder during the critical strategy phase. What if I already have a product idea, do I still need this? + Absolutely! Having an idea is just the starting point. We help you validate if people actually want what you’re planning to build, identify the core features that drive adoption, prioritize your roadmap for maximum impact, and create detailed specifications developers can work from. Most ‘great ideas’ change significantly once they meet real users. How do you ensure I don't build the wrong product? + We use lean validation methods including user interviews, landing page tests, prototype validation, vibe-coded prototypes, competitive analysis, and market research. We test assumptions before committing to development. By the time we’re done, you’ll have real user feedback, validated demand signals, and a roadmap based on actual market needs, not just assumptions. What exactly do I get at the end of this engagement? + You get a complete product development package: validated product roadmap with prioritized features, detailed user stories and technical requirements, proven Product-Market Fit signals, competitive positioning strategy, and everything your development team needs to start building immediately. Essentially, a blueprint for building the right product. What if my product direction changes during the process? + That’s exactly what this phase is for! Direction changes are normal and healthy, it means we’re learning and adapting based on real market feedback. We help you navigate pivots strategically, ensuring changes are data-driven rather than guesswork. Many successful products look different from their initial concept. How does this connect to your development services? + This is the essential first step in our 3-stage journey. Once your product strategy is solid, you can seamlessly transition to our Software Development phase with a clear roadmap and validated requirements. This saves you the typical 2.5k€ discovery phase since we’ve already done the strategic groundwork. Alternatively, we can also just start with the Discovery phase and develop right away. How long does it take to get clear product direction? + Most clients see initial clarity within 2-3 weeks, with a solid, validated roadmap typically ready in 4-6 weeks. However, we work until the direction is genuinely clear and validated, we don’t operate on fixed timelines but on achieving the right outcomes. You can cancel anytime and get last week refunded if you’re not seeing progress. What if I need ongoing product strategy support after development starts? + Sure, we can continue providing strategic product guidance while also ensuring your development stays on track. Many clients benefit from ongoing product strategy support as they learn from real users and need to evolve their roadmap. When should a startup hire a fractional co-founder vs a full-time CTO? + Fractional fits pre-seed or seed when paying a full-time CTO would burn 30-40% of your runway and you don’t yet need 40 hours/week of strategy. It also fits non-technical founders shipping their first version, where one fractional partner replaces three hires (product, technical lead, dev). You move to full-time when the product needs deep daily decisions, the team is large enough to need management, or fundraising requires a named full-time technical co-founder. We’ll tell you when you’ve outgrown fractional. Talk to an expert Get in touch → Ship sooner. Bet smaller. Scale smarter. © Wavect GmbH. pages.text: Top 19 RWA Tokenization Companies in 2026 | Aegas.io Site navigation Get in touch Services Portfolio Blog Contact us Get in touch Get in touch <== Back to all articles Top 19 RWA Tokenization Companies in 2026: Platforms vs. Engineering Vendors 29 Jul 26 / 5 min read Nineteen firms rank for 'top RWA tokenization companies', and they are two different jobs: 9 hold the licences your asset needs, 10 build the software around them. This guide ranks both. Michael Su (CEO) Summarise with Last updated: July 29, 2026 TL;DR. If you've ever looked for "RWA tokenization companies to tokenize your asset," you're choosing between two kinds of companies. A regulated issuance platform holds the license your asset needs to trade legally (a transfer agent, broker-dealer, or exchange registration): Securitize, Ondo Finance, ADDX, Bitbond, and tZERO hold one directly, while Tokeny and Polymesh supply the infrastructure underneath rather than the license itself. An engineering vendor (Aegas, Antier, Suffescom, LeewayHertz and a dozen similar firms) builds the system around it: investor portal, KYC, custody, corporate-actions logic. Most teams need both, platform first. The vendor tier below is ranked by work you can open and check. The freshest inputs here are from late July 2026: Securitize Capital LLC's SEC investment adviser registration on top of its transfer agent and broker-dealer status, and roughly $34 billion in on-chain distributed RWA value. That figure moves week to week; don't quote it as fixed. Do you need a tokenization platform or a development team? This guide is for the team that already has the asset, a fund or a property portfolio, and now looks to get it issued and trading on-chain in a compliant manner. Before comparing names, settle one question: who holds the license your asset needs? One question decides whether you need a platform, an engineering vendor, or both, platform first You need a platform when nobody holds it yet: a transfer agent who can maintain the share register, a broker-dealer with an ATS for secondary trading, an investor registry that enforces who can hold the token. Securitize, ADDX, and Bitbond all sell this, and Tokeny supplies the infrastructure under it. You need an engineering vendor once that relationship exists and what's missing is the system around it: the investor portal, the KYC integration, custody, corporate actions. Our RWA tokenization development page walks through that fork before either conversation starts. What's the difference between a white-label tokenization platform and a custom build? White-label means you license a platform's stack (Securitize's or Tokeny's infrastructure, ADDX's exchange) and plug your asset into rules someone else wrote. You supply the asset and, usually, the regulatory relationship. It is faster and cheaper because the compliance logic already exists and has cleared a regulator. The cost is control: you inherit the platform's reporting format, its data model, and its reading of whichever standard it runs. A custom build means an engineering vendor writes the smart contracts and compliance logic to your specifications. It costs more and takes longer, since nothing is pre-cleared, but keeps corporate actions, forced transfers, and jurisdiction-specific rules yours. Blockchain App Factory, Debut Infotech, and Omisoft all publish near-identical white-label-versus-custom comparisons, and none names the actual fork criterion: whether you already hold, or can acquire, the regulatory relationship a white-label platform requires. Without it, white-label is the only fast path, since custom still needs someone downstream to hold the license. With it, or if the platform's rules don't fit your asset, custom is the only way to keep the logic yours. Our blockchain development company selection guidance covers the rest. Conflating the vendor question with the platform question is how buyers end up with someone who can write Solidity but has never touched a transfer-agent relationship. Which regulated issuance platforms hold up in 2026? Platform Regulator / license Token standard Model TVL or AUM (source, date) Securitize SEC: transfer agent, broker-dealer/ATS, plus (Securitize Capital LLC) investment adviser, registered Jul 22, 2026 Multi-chain issuance; no single public standard Acts as transfer agent $4.39B [Chainstack, 2026-07-08] Tokeny No regulator held directly; infrastructure used by regulated issuers ERC-3643 (T-REX), originated by Tokeny Infra/tooling: on-chain identity registry $32B+ tokenized under the standard (vendor-claimed, Tokeny/Chainalysis) Polymesh No single financial regulator named; node operators must be licensed financial entities; SOC 2 Type 1 (2025) Native Polymesh protocol Infra/tooling: permissioned L1 Not disclosed Zoniqx None named DyCIST / ERC-7518 Infra/tooling: asset lifecycle management (TALM) Not disclosed Centrifuge None named Protocol-specific; no single public standard confirmed Infra/tooling: tokenized private-credit pools $1.64B [Chainstack, 2026-07-08] Ondo Finance FINRA clearance (2026) for tokenized stocks/ETFs to US investors Not a single named standard in materials reviewed Issuer: tokenized Treasuries, money-market exposure $3.62B [Chainstack, 2026-07-08] ADDX Singapore MAS: Capital Markets Services Licensee, Recognised Market Operator, Exempt Financial Adviser (CMS100798, since 2020) Not disclosed Regulated market operator / issuer Not disclosed Bitbond BaFin (Germany); first BaFin-approved tokenized-bond prospectus (BB1); issuance under eWpG, Luxembourg fund regimes, EU DLT Pilot Regime Publishes own ERC-1400/ERC-3643 comparison; no single default confirmed Issuer under BaFin oversight Not disclosed tZERO / Archax tZERO: SEC-registered, FINRA-member broker-dealer (US). Archax: FCA-regulated (UK) Not disclosed Split model: tZERO distribution/custody, Archax issuance/lifecycle (GOVY, partnership since Jun 23, 2026) Not disclosed The platform table below only includes platforms that clear one of two bars: a named regulator or license, or a formalized token standard with disclosed adoption. TVL and AUM figures carry a source and date, since these numbers move weekly, and several platforms don't publish one at all. The figures for Securitize, Ondo Finance, and Centrifuge come from Chainstack's July 8, 2026 platform comparison . Securitize is the one entry with a complete regulatory stack. Securitize Capital LLC registered with the SEC as an investment adviser effective July 22, 2026, on top of the existing transfer agent and broker-dealer/ATS registrations. That puts four regulated functions under one roof (transfer agent, broker-dealer/ATS, investment adviser, fund administration), a combination no other platform here holds. Tokeny sits at the opposite end: infrastructure rather than a regulated entity in the Securitize sense. Its T-REX engine enforces compliance inside the token contract rather than through a company acting as transfer agent. Whether Tokeny itself ever takes on a transfer-agent role is unclear, so this table doesn't claim it either way. What's confirmed is an identity-registry architecture used by DTCC, Apex Group, Invesco, Franklin Templeton, and Fasanara Capital . One number gets conflated across almost every competing list. rwa.xyz's "distributed" value , tokens issued and freely tradable on-chain, sat around $34.67 billion as of late July 2026, down from a $35.2 billion peak on July 10, 2026. Its separate "represented" figure, assets committed to tokenization but not yet tradable, runs $218 billion to $388 billion. A platform citing a market "worth $300 billion" likely means represented value, which says nothing about whether an investor can exit a position. If your asset needs institutional settlement rather than retail-style secondary trading, Canton Network is a different lane. Fireblocks added Canton Coin custody support in February 2026. That DAML-based permissioned settlement model is what our Canton Network development page covers. Which engineering vendors can build the integration layer, and how do you read their claims? Company Founded Independent rating & reviews Production work you can open and check Aegas 2017 Clutch 4.9/5 (15 reviews), GoodFirms 5.0/5, TechBehemoths 5.0/5, DesignRush 4.7/5 Yes. Privex , a perpetuals DEX on Base and Coti: $22B in platform volume to date, 8M executed trades. Nest DEX , a ve(3,3) AMM on HyperEVM: $2.43B cumulative volume , still maintained by the team that built it. DeFi trading systems, not tokenized securities, and the section below says what that doesn't prove Antier Solutions 2011 Clutch profile exists, 48 reviews; score not retrieved No named, openable production system found. Headcount 700-738 (LeadIQ and own marketing disagree); "15+ years" self-reported; ranks itself in its own list Suffescom Solutions Not confirmed Clutch: 108-117 reviews across a paginated listing; score not retrieved None found. Ranks itself #1 on its own published list LeewayHertz 2007, San Francisco Clutch 4.7/5 (9 reviews); GoodFirms 5.0/5 (5 reviews) None found. Headcount disputed: PitchBook 300, Tracxn 182 (May 2026), same company PixelPlex 2007 (own claim) Clutch profile exists, 33 reviews; score not retrieved None found. "80+ projects", "$500M in client revenue raised", "1M+ smart contract executions", all self-reported SoluLab 2014 (own claim) Review count not retrieved None found. "1,500+ projects, 500+ clients" self-reported Debut Infotech Not confirmed Not confirmed None found. Marketing-page claims only Blocktunix Not confirmed (Crunchbase profile exists) Clutch "Foremost Blockchain Development Firm in UAE" mention; count not retrieved None found. Marketing-page claims only Hivelance Not confirmed Not confirmed None found. Marketing-page claims only Blockchain App Factory Not confirmed Not confirmed None found. "12+ years of expertise" self-reported The agency tier holds no licenses to check, so the usual proof is a directory profile, and the directories disagree with each other. That leaves one test that works: can you open the software the vendor built, today, and see it running with real money moving through it? A platform's license doesn't get you an investor portal, and most competing lists blur the two tiers: Suffescom's "Top 10" post ranks Securitize, a dev shop, an RPC provider, and itself on the same numbered list , with no category label at all. We publish this list and we're on it, at the top. So is nearly everyone else who publishes one: Suffescom ranks itself #1 on its own list from January 15, 2026, and Antier places itself second on its own list , behind Securitize. The difference we'd ask you to hold us to is the last column. Every figure in the Aegas row is either a live URL you can open now or a rating on a third-party profile you can check yourself. Apply that standard to our row and to whoever is on your shortlist. LeewayHertz's headcount is reported as 300 employees by PitchBook and 182 by Tracxn , a 65% spread between two paid directories describing the same company at the same time. Company numbers on directory pages are compiled, not audited. A vendor quoting "300+ engineers" is repeating a figure two directories can't agree on. Most of the rest of this table offers project counts and client counts with nothing behind them. "None found" means a named, currently-reachable production system was not found in the company's own published materials during this research. Several of these firms have almost certainly shipped work under NDA, which is a real constraint. The point is what a buyer can verify before signing. Why Aegas sits at the top of its own table, and where that evidence stops. Since 2017 the team has shipped 100+ projects. The two in the table are trading systems: Privex, a perpetuals DEX at $22B platform volume and 8M trades over two years, and Nest DEX, a ve(3,3) AMM at $2.43B cumulative volume on HyperEVM. They do not prove investor-facing compliance reporting or a KYC-vendor integration, because neither project needed them. If a vendor's cited work is DeFi trading, ask specifically how they'd handle the pieces that only appear in a regulated context: corporate actions, forced transfers, and an identity registry your KYC provider has to feed. Ask us that too. Contracts go to third-party auditors by name (Hacken, OpenZeppelin, Trail of Bits, Halborn, CertiK, Sherlock). Aegas isn't a transfer agent or any other regulated entity, so the license comes from the platform table, and it isn't an audit firm; it coordinates audits with the firms named above. A vendor who blurs either line is worth a harder look. How do you choose a vendor? Start with the disqualifiers. Every name in the vendor table above, and most that didn't make it, will say yes to "have you built RWA tokenization before." That question eliminates no one. The eight below do, each answerable inside a single scoping call. Can they name the regulator and license number behind a compliance claim? Naming one separates a regulatory relationship from a feature description. Will they produce a reference client who'll take a call? NDA-bound and shuttered projects are real constraints, but zero references across every engagement is a different signal. On a platform deal, can they say who is the transfer agent of record, them or the platform? A vendor who can't answer that in one sentence doesn't understand what they're building. Is "12+ years of experience" backed by one checkable detail, a chain, a timeline, an outcome? Can they explain how corporate actions work on the standard they're proposing: a dividend, a forced transfer, a redemption? Reaching for the whitepaper instead of a plain answer is the tell. Will they quote one flat price before scoping custody integration and which KYC vendor they'll connect? A number that early means the scope isn't defined yet. Are they conflating "we support ERC-3643" with "we're a registered transfer agent"? A compliant smart contract is not authorization to maintain an official investor register. If contracts are already live, which third-party firm audited them: Hacken, OpenZeppelin, Trail of Bits, Halborn, CertiK, Sherlock, or one you haven't heard of? Calling an internal review "the audit" is a different thing. None of the competing lists (Finextra, Suffescom, Antier, Blockchain App Factory) publishes anything like this, because each is a vendor or a vendor-adjacent host with a stake in its own ranking. Which token standard should you use: ERC-3643, ERC-1400, or CMTAT? ERC-3643, known as T-REX, is the standard behind Tokeny's infrastructure: compliance rules live in the token contract itself, so a non-compliant transfer fails at the contract level. Tokeny's own figures put adoption at over $32 billion tokenized across 180-plus jurisdictions , a vendor-claimed figure, not an independent audit. ISO certification for the standard was reported in progress as of May 2026, not finalized; several sources frame it as a prerequisite for sovereign-wealth-fund and pension-manager adoption. ERC-1400 is older and relies on off-chain checks rather than an on-chain identity registry. Bitbond's own published comparison frames it as stronger on operational flexibility, with ERC-3643 stronger on auditability at the cost of gas and complexity. One secondary source calls ERC-1400 "the more practical choice for the majority of RWA projects in 2026," against the ERC-3643-dominance narrative coming from Tokeny-adjacent sources. Make whichever vendor you're evaluating justify the choice in specifics (gas cost, jurisdiction, the exact compliance behavior needed) rather than accepting "3643 is the standard now" as settled fact. CMTAT is Swiss, from the Capital Markets and Technology Association, and chain-agnostic by design rather than written as an ERC. Its reference implementation is Solidity , built on OpenZeppelin for EVM chains including Ethereum, with a separate Solana implementation, so "not an ERC" doesn't mean "not available on Ethereum." Its stated advantage is native support for debt-based tokens and forced trades, which ERC-3643 and ERC-1400 handle less cleanly. If the asset is a bond or structured product, CMTAT is worth putting on the table. Watch one more figure. The $1.2 trillion tokenized-securities market number attributed to analyst firm Digital Asset Research and cited on Bitbond's standards page likely counts committed or represented value under a broader securities definition, well above the roughly $34 billion actually trading on-chain. Competing pages put both numbers in the same paragraph, which would have you planning a build for a market roughly 35 times larger than the real one. Standard choice drives build cost and timeline, which our token engineering and launch service treats as a first decision to lock. How much does the integration layer cost? The cost guides on this topic, Octal Software , Antier , and Pixel Web Solutions , all price one thing: building a tokenization platform from scratch, usually $100,000 to $3 million depending on scope. None prices what most buyers actually need: the integration layer around a platform they've already licensed. The platform license prices easily; these five components are what an integration quote has to scope That layer is separate from whatever Securitize, Tokeny, or ADDX charges for the platform itself: an investor portal your holders log into, compliance-ready reporting and dashboards, corporate-actions handling for redemption and forced transfers, custody and payment-rail integration wired to your custodian or bank, and a KYC integration linking the platform's identity registry to whoever runs your investor due diligence. None of that has one honest number, because it scales with how many rails and vendors you're connecting. A quote call should establish three things: how many custody or payment rails need integrating; how many KYC vendors are in play, your existing provider or the platform's own or both; and whether the corporate-actions logic is templated against the platform's structure or fully custom because your asset's redemption rules don't fit. A vendor who answers those three specifically is quoting a scope. One who skips straight to a number is quoting a guess. Our blockchain integration services coverage goes deeper on the integration work, which is where most of the budget goes. This is the work Aegas is set up to quote, scoped from your rails and your KYC provider rather than a template. Our RWA tokenization development page is the tokenization-specific version of that conversation. Aegas perspective. What breaks, in engineering terms, when a licensed platform meets a live investor base is rarely the smart contract itself. More often it's the seam between the platform's identity registry and whichever KYC vendor the client already ran, or a corporate-actions rule the template doesn't cover because it was built for the platform's median customer, not this specific asset. None of it shows up on a platform's marketing page, because solving it was never the platform's job; that work falls to the buyer, or whoever gets hired to build the layer around the license. Michael Su, co-founder, Aegas So, platform, agency, or both? If the missing piece is the license or the transfer-agent relationship, start with whichever entry in the platform table holds the relationship your asset needs. If that's settled and what's missing is the system around it, pick an engineering vendor against the disqualifiers above rather than off a self-ranked top-10 post. When you get to the engineering half, run the disqualifiers on us. Ask which auditor signed the contracts and who the transfer agent of record is on your deal, then ask for the reference call. Open Privex and Nest DEX and see whether the answers match what's running. Tell us what you're tokenizing and we'll scope the layer around it. About the author. Michael Su is co-founder of Aegas, a blockchain engineering agency that builds smart contracts, DeFi protocols, and tokenization systems. Our RWA tokenization development page walks through that fork before either conversation starts."}},{"@type":"Question","name":"What's the difference between a white-label tokenization platform and a custom build?","acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"White-label means you license a platform's stack (Securitize's or Tokeny's infrastructure, ADDX's exchange) and plug your asset into rules someone else wrote. You supply the asset and, usually, the regulatory relationship. It is faster and cheaper because the compliance logic already exists and has cleared a regulator. The cost is control: you inherit the platform's reporting format, its data model, and its reading of whichever standard it runs.

A custom build means an engineering vendor writes the smart contracts and compliance logic to your specifications. It costs more and takes longer, since nothing is pre-cleared, but keeps corporate actions, forced transfers, and jurisdiction-specific rules yours.

Blockchain App Factory, Debut Infotech, and Omisoft all publish near-identical white-label-versus-custom comparisons, and none names the actual fork criterion: whether you already hold, or can acquire, the regulatory relationship a white-label platform requires. Without it, white-label is the only fast path, since custom still needs someone downstream to hold the license."}},{"@type":"Question","name":"Which regulated issuance platforms hold up in 2026?","acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"The platform table below only includes platforms that clear one of two bars: a named regulator or license, or a formalized token standard with disclosed adoption. TVL and AUM figures carry a source and date, since these numbers move weekly, and several platforms don't publish one at all. The figures for Securitize, Ondo Finance, and Centrifuge come from Chainstack's July 8, 2026 platform comparison.

Securitize is the one entry with a complete regulatory stack. Securitize Capital LLC registered with the SEC as an investment adviser effective July 22, 2026, on top of the existing transfer agent and broker-dealer/ATS registrations. That puts four regulated functions under one roof (transfer agent, broker-dealer/ATS, investment adviser, fund administration), a combination no other platform here holds.

Tokeny sits at the opposite end: infrastructure rather than a regulated entity in the Securitize sense. Its T-REX engine enforces compliance inside the token contract rather than through a company acting as transfer agent. Whether Tokeny itself ever takes on a transfer-agent role is unclear, so this table doesn't claim it either way."}},{"@type":"Question","name":"Which engineering vendors can build the integration layer, and how do you read their claims?","acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"The agency tier holds no licenses to check, so the usual proof is a directory profile, and the directories disagree with each other. That leaves one test that works: can you open the software the vendor built, today, and see it running with real money moving through it? A platform's license doesn't get you an investor portal, and most competing lists blur the two tiers: Suffescom's "Top 10" post ranks Securitize, a dev shop, an RPC provider, and itself on the same numbered list, with no category label at all.

We publish this list and we're on it, at the top. So is nearly everyone else who publishes one: Suffescom ranks itself #1 on its own list from January 15, 2026, and Antier places itself second on its own list, behind Securitize. The difference we'd ask you to hold us to is the last column. Every figure in the Aegas row is either a live URL you can open now or a rating on a third-party profile you can check yourself. Apply that standard to our row and to whoever is on your shortlist.

LeewayHertz's headcount is reported as 300 employees by PitchBook and 182 by Tracxn, a 65% spread between two paid directories describing the same company at the same time."}},{"@type":"Question","name":"Which token standard should you use: ERC-3643, ERC-1400, or CMTAT?","acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"ERC-3643, known as T-REX, is the standard behind Tokeny's infrastructure: compliance rules live in the token contract itself, so a non-compliant transfer fails at the contract level. Tokeny's own figures put adoption at over $32 billion tokenized across 180-plus jurisdictions, a vendor-claimed figure, not an independent audit. ISO certification for the standard was reported in progress as of May 2026, not finalized; several sources frame it as a prerequisite for sovereign-wealth-fund and pension-manager adoption.

ERC-1400 is older and relies on off-chain checks rather than an on-chain identity registry. Bitbond's own published comparison frames it as stronger on operational flexibility, with ERC-3643 stronger on auditability at the cost of gas and complexity. One secondary source calls ERC-1400 "the more practical choice for the majority of RWA projects in 2026," against the ERC-3643-dominance narrative coming from Tokeny-adjacent sources."}},{"@type":"Question","name":"How much does the integration layer cost?","acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"The cost guides on this topic, Octal Software, Antier, and Pixel Web Solutions, all price one thing: building a tokenization platform from scratch, usually $100,000 to $3 million depending on scope. None prices what most buyers actually need: the integration layer around a platform they've already licensed.

The platform license prices easily; these five components are what an integration quote has to scope

That layer is separate from whatever Securitize, Tokeny, or ADDX charges for the platform itself: an investor portal your holders log into, compliance-ready reporting and dashboards, corporate-actions handling for redemption and forced transfers, custody and payment-rail integration wired to your custodian or bank, and a KYC integration linking the platform's identity registry to whoever runs your investor due diligence.

None of that has one honest number, because it scales with how many rails and vendors you're connecting."}},{"@type":"Question","name":"So, platform, agency, or both?","acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"If the missing piece is the license or the transfer-agent relationship, start with whichever entry in the platform table holds the relationship your asset needs. If that's settled and what's missing is the system around it, pick an engineering vendor against the disqualifiers above rather than off a self-ranked top-10 post.

When you get to the engineering half, run the disqualifiers on us. Ask which auditor signed the contracts and who the transfer agent of record is on your deal, then ask for the reference call. Open Privex and Nest DEX and see whether the answers match what's running. Tell us what you're tokenizing and we'll scope the layer around it."}}]}

Richiedi Preventivo Tutti i temi Note operative 01 Problemi concreti, non contenuti generici. 02 Priorita', rischi e tradeoff spiegati con chiarezza. 03 Focus su processi, adozione e impatto sul business. Aree tematiche Sviluppo software personalizzato 01 Sviluppo software personalizzato 02 ERP e gestionali 03 Sviluppo app 04 AI per aziende 05 IoT e integrazioni hardware/software In evidenza Sales operations Sviluppo software personalizzato 26 giugno 2026 7 min lettura Software gestione preventivi B2B: quando sviluppare e quando integrare Quando preventivi, follow-up e revisioni passano tra email, CRM e fogli, il problema non e solo commerciale: e un workflow operativo da rendere leggibile. Apri l'articolo Strategia digitale Sviluppo software personalizzato 20 marzo 2026 8 min lettura Quando lo sviluppo software personalizzato crea davvero vantaggio competitivo Molte aziende sanno di avere processi inefficienti, ma non sempre capiscono quando convenga costruire software su misura invece di forzare strumenti generici. Apri l'articolo SaaS custom Sviluppo software personalizzato 26 giugno 2026 7 min lettura Sviluppo piattaforma SaaS: quando costruire e quando integrare strumenti esistenti Una piattaforma SaaS custom ha senso quando prodotto, workflow, ruoli e modello di business richiedono una base proprietaria, non solo una dashboard. Apri l'articolo Partner software Sviluppo software personalizzato 15 giugno 2026 7 min lettura Come valutare una software house prima di avviare un progetto su misura Scegliere una software house non significa confrontare solo portfolio e prezzo. Serve capire se il partner sa leggere il processo, ridurre il rischio e trasformare vincoli reali in software utile. Apri l'articolo Ultimi articoli Ultimi articoli Contenuti pensati per chi deve decidere cosa integrare, rifare, automatizzare o semplificare. Pagina 1 / 1 Software su misura Sviluppo software personalizzato 10 giugno 2026 7 min lettura Dati scollegati, Excel e workaround: quando il software su misura diventa la scelta più onesta Fogli Excel, esportazioni e controlli manuali spesso non sono il problema: sono il sintomo di un processo che è cresciuto più degli strumenti che lo sostengono. Apri l'articolo Software operativo Sviluppo software personalizzato 4 giugno 2026 7 min lettura Preventivi B2B lenti o poco tracciati: quando serve un flusso software dedicato Molte aziende percepiscono il problema prima di riuscire a definirlo: lead, preventivi, follow-up e dati cliente sparsi tra CRM, email e fogli. Questa bozza aiuta a capire quando ha senso intervenire con software, integrazioni o automazioni. Apri l'articolo Delivery Sviluppo software personalizzato 31 marzo 2026 8 min lettura Discovery tecnica: cosa deve uscire prima di iniziare a sviluppare La discovery non serve a rallentare il progetto. Serve a evitare che il team inizi a sviluppare con troppe assunzioni sbagliate e poca chiarezza sul valore reale. Apri l'articolo Operations Sviluppo software personalizzato 31 marzo 2026 7 min lettura Dati scollegati, fogli Excel e workaround: i segnali che chiedono software custom Il problema non e' Excel in se'. Il problema e' quando Excel, email e strumenti scollegati diventano il collante invisibile del lavoro. Apri l'articolo Legacy Systems Sviluppo software personalizzato 31 marzo 2026 8 min lettura Software legacy: quando integrare, quando rifare, quando fermarsi Non tutto il software legacy va riscritto. Il punto e' capire quando l'integrazione regge, quando il refactor basta e quando continuare a rattoppare costa piu' di una nuova base. Apri l'articolo DG Technologies Idee pratiche per trasformare complessita' digitale in sistemi piu' chiari. Analisi operative su software custom, ERP, applicazioni, AI e integrazioni. Ogni articolo parte da un problema reale e arriva a una decisione tecnica piu' semplice da prendere. Working software every two weeks. 01 Plan Before writing code, we work with you to understand the opportunity, define the product goal, align stakeholders, and reduce the risk of building the wrong thing. We help shape the roadmap, technical approach and feature priorities so the product has a strong foundation from day one. What happens Define the product goal, users and core value proposition Prioritise features into practical release stages Map the high-level system architecture and integrations Validate technical feasibility, risks and delivery approach Identify the right tools, platforms and partners Create prototypes, flows or designs where needed Outcome ✓ A clear product direction ✓ Aligned stakeholders and priorities ✓ A practical roadmap for delivery ✓ Tangible artefacts such as prototypes, designs or technical planning docs 02 Build Once the direction is clear, our team moves into delivery with a focus on momentum, visibility and adaptability. We build in stages so you can see progress early, give feedback often, and make informed decisions as the product evolves. What happens Dedicated specialists across front end, back end, smart contracts and cloud Milestone-based delivery with regular demos and progress reporting Continuous collaboration and feedback loops Clear visibility over progress, blockers and trade-offs Flexible involvement depending on how hands-on you want to be Working features delivered incrementally, not all at the end Outcome ✓ A product that becomes usable step by step ✓ Faster learning through real feedback ✓ Clear visibility over what is built, what is next and why ✓ A roadmap that can evolve as the product matures 03 Assure We treat quality assurance, security and technical review as part of the build, not an afterthought. From smart contract review practices to QA across the application stack, we focus on shipping with confidence. What happens Code review and multi-level technical oversight QA across core user flows and critical system behaviour Automated testing where appropriate Smart contract and Web3-specific review practices Pre-audit preparation and internal review for blockchain systems Validation of release readiness before production deployment Outcome ✓ Greater confidence in quality and security ✓ Clearer visibility over risks and outstanding issues ✓ A product that is better prepared for real users and real usage 04 Launch Launching is not just a handover moment. We support the release process with the right planning, environments, deployment controls and monitoring so the product can go live safely and continue evolving. pages.text: Glamsterdam: what's next for Ethereum | Labrys Skip to content Services Projects Insights About Us Toggle theme Let's Talk Toggle theme Home Insights Glamsterdam: what's next for Ethereum Blog Post Glamsterdam: what's next for Ethereum Glamsterdam is the biggest structural change to Ethereum since the Merge. Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation, Block-Level Access Lists, and a protocol-layer fix for the MEV and censorship problem mevWatch has been tracking since 2022. Ethereum L2 Rollups MEV Protocol Upgrades Staking Luke Shulver | 22 May 2026 | 6 mins Insight Luke Shulver | 22 May 2026 | 6 mins Key takeaways ✓ Glamsterdam is targeting late Q3 2026 and is the biggest structural change to Ethereum since the Merge. ✓ EIP-7732 (ePBS) moves MEV and censorship-resistance from a social trust assumption to a protocol guarantee. Researchers estimate up to a 70% drop in MEV extraction. ✓ EIP-7928 (Block-Level Access Lists) require blocks to pre-declare which accounts and storage slots they touch. That unlocks parallel execution and a real path toward 10,000 TPS on L1. ✓ Paired with a proposed gas limit increase from 60M up to 200M, this compounds the cheaper L2 data settlement that Dencun started. ✓ The risks are real. Client coordination is hard, solo stakers could be pushed further out, and relay-layer concentration could just re-emerge one layer deeper at the builder layer. Contents 01 Intro 02 A quick refresher on where we've been 03 Glamsterdam: target date and what's in it 04 Why it matters 05 Where it could go wrong 06 Looking past Glamsterdam 07 Glamsterdam Resources Glamsterdam is the biggest structural change to Ethereum since the Merge. It brings enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation, Block-Level Access Lists, and a protocol-layer fix for the MEV and censorship problem mevWatch has been tracking since 2022. 01 Intro Ethereum's release cadence has quietly become one of the more predictable things in crypto. After years of "soon," core devs have settled into a rhythm of roughly two hard forks per year, each shipping a tightly scoped bundle of EIPs aimed at the same end state: a credibly neutral, censorship-resistant settlement layer with enough scaling headroom to actually be useful. With Pectra behind us and Fusaka activated in December, attention has turned to Glamsterdam, the next mainnet upgrade. It's also the biggest structural change to Ethereum since the Merge, particularly if you've been following the MEV and censorship-resistance conversation on mevWatch , the dashboard we built and maintain to track OFAC-compliant block production on Ethereum. Glamsterdam is the upgrade that finally addresses, at the protocol level, the exact problem mevWatch has been measuring since the Merge. 02 A quick refresher on where we've been Before getting into Glamsterdam, it's worth grounding ourselves in the post-Merge timeline, because the trajectory matters. The Merge (September 2022) moved Ethereum from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake. Energy use collapsed, the issuance curve flipped, and the door opened to everything since. Shapella (April 2023) finally enabled withdrawals for staked ETH. The missing piece that turned staking from a one-way commitment into a legitimate yield product. Dencun (March 2024) shipped EIP-4844 and proto-danksharding. Blob space made rollup data orders of magnitude cheaper, which is the single biggest reason L2 fees collapsed to fractions of a cent. We wrote about it here at the time. Pectra (May 2025) bundled 11 EIPs across both the consensus and execution layers. Account abstraction via EIP-7702, larger validator effective balances, and improved blob throughput were the standout shifts. Our take on Pectra is here . Fusaka (December 2025) then delivered PeerDAS (EIP-7594): Peer data availability sampling, the protocol's first real step toward full danksharding alongside a block gas limit bump from ~36M to 60M, a per-transaction gas cap (EIP-7825) for DoS hardening, and secp256r1 support (EIP-7951), which is the unsexy but important EIP that makes passkey and device-native signing viable on Ethereum. Which brings us to Glamsterdam. 03 Glamsterdam: target date and what's in it Glamsterdam (a portmanteau of Gloas for the consensus layer and Amsterdam for the execution layer) is targeting late Q3 2026 for mainnet activation. We'll dive into the two headliner EIPs confirmed, as both are structural changes to how blocks are produced and validated. EIP-7732 | Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS) If you've followed the MEV conversation over the last few years, you know that the role of "block builder" and "block proposer" has been split in practice since the Merge, but the split has been held together by an out-of-protocol piece of middleware called MEV-Boost, run by trusted relays. It works, but it concentrates power in a small number of relay operators, and it's been a persistent source of censorship concerns. Back in 2022, we built mevWatch to raise awareness this very problem, and recently gave the site a fresh redesign. In the months after the Merge, the share of OFAC-compliant blocks (blocks built by relays that filter sanctioned transactions, primarily Tornado Cash-related) climbed past 70% before community pressure, and the rise of non-censoring relays like Ultra Sound, Agnostic, and Aestus, pulled it back. mevWatch has tracked that figure block-by-block ever since, and it remains the clearest real-time picture of how much of Ethereum's block space is being filtered by U.S. regulatory compliance at the relay layer. It's a useful number, but it's also a workaround. Validators having to choose the right relay is a social-layer fix to what should be a protocol-layer guarantee. Snapshot from the newly redesigned mevWatch dashboard. ePBS takes the proposer/builder separation and enshrines it in the protocol itself . Proposers (who choose which block goes next) and builders (who assemble the actual execution payload) exchange blocks and payment through rules the chain enforces directly, with no third-party relay required. The expected outcomes are meaningful: researchers estimate MEV extraction drops by up to 70%, the data propagation window expands from ~2 seconds to ~9 seconds (unlocking higher throughput and more blob capacity), and Ethereum becomes materially harder to censor at the relay layer because there is no relay layer . For anyone running validators, this is a real change to the staking economics and operational profile. For everyone else, it's the upgrade that finally moves MEV and censorship-resistance from a social trust assumption to a protocol guarantee. EIP-7928: Block-Level Access Lists (BALs) The second headliner is less philosophically charged but arguably more important for day-to-day scaling. Today, when a block is executed, validators discover which accounts and storage slots are touched as transactions run, sequentially. That's a hard constraint on parallel execution and a major contributor to worst-case block validation time. BALs require blocks to pre-declare which accounts and storage slots will be read or written. With that information available up front, clients can fetch state in parallel, validate transactions in parallel, and pipeline execution far more efficiently. It's the foundation for a credible push toward 10,000 TPS on L1, and it pairs with a proposed block gas limit increase from 60M to as high as 200M. 04 Why it matters The shorthand for Glamsterdam is "scaling and MEV reform", but it's worth unpacking who actually benefits. For L2s and rollup users , the combination of BALs, a higher gas limit, and the longer propagation window from ePBS means materially more blob capacity and cheaper data settlement. We've already seen what cheaper data does to L2 fees post-Dencun, fractions of a cent on the major rollups, and the use cases we predicted in 2023 (high-frequency gaming, on-chain order books, mainstream payments) actually shipping. Glamsterdam compounds that. The journey EIP-4844 started in March 2024 is the same one the protocol is still running on, more bandwidth, less friction, more headroom for the use cases that the old "blockchains can't scale" argument used to gatekeep. For traders and DeFi users , ePBS is the big one. Less extractable MEV means less sandwich attacks, less hidden tax on swaps, and pricing that better reflects the actual market. The censorship-resistance improvements also matter to anyone touching protocols that have historically been sanctioned-address-adjacent, and the OFAC-compliant block share should, in principle, become a much less meaningful metric once ePBS removes the relay chokepoint that creates it. For consumer apps and onchain UX , the parallel execution unlocked by BALs is the path to L1 actually feeling responsive at scale. Combined with secp256r1 from Fusaka, the building blocks for genuinely mainstream Web3 UX, passkeys, account abstraction, fast confirmations, predictable fees, are now all in place or imminent. For institutional stakers and validator operators , the move away from MEV-Boost relays simplifies the trust model. Fewer external dependencies, fewer points of failure, fewer compliance questions about which relay you're routing through. 05 Where it could go wrong Glamsterdam is structurally ambitious, and the bullish read deserves a counterweight. ePBS adds real consensus-layer complexity, new slot structure, new attestation rules, new economic flows between proposers and builders, and coordinating five execution clients (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Reth, Erigon) and five consensus clients (Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar) on changes this deep is genuinely hard. Slippage from H1 into late 2026 is a real possibility, and adding FOCIL or other non-headliner EIPs only widens that window. BALs also add a per-block computational burden on block producers, and the combination of more sophisticated builders and BAL overhead could quietly push solo stakers further to the margins, the opposite of what the upgrade is meant to protect. There's also a subtler question on the MEV side. The headline "up to 70% MEV reduction" estimate assumes a competitive builder market post-activation. If a handful of sophisticated builders end up dominating the on-chain auction, the relay-layer concentration mevWatch currently tracks could simply re-emerge one layer deeper, at the builder layer instead. The protocol guarantees a fair auction; it doesn't guarantee a decentralised set of bidders. None of this is a reason not to ship Glamsterdam, but it is a reason to read the post-activation data carefully before declaring victory. 06 Looking past Glamsterdam The next upgrade, Hegotá, is expected to bring on FOCIL and Verkle trees as headliners, and we'll cover them later in the year. Together, Fusaka, Glamsterdam, and Hegotá form the most aggressive 18-month stretch of protocol-layer change Ethereum has ever attempted. The takeaway is that Ethereum is shipping, on a cadence, against a coherent roadmap. The through-line from EIP-4844 in 2024 to Glamsterdam in 2026 is consistent. More bandwidth, less friction, credibly neutral block production. For teams building on Ethereum, that's the signal worth paying attention to, not the price chart. REVIEWS TEAM BLOG BOOK NOW Development Why Vibe Coding and Shipping Faster Can Make It Hard For Your UX to Keep Up Alex Doukas 14 September 2026 Quick answer: AI-powered product development is accelerating how fast teams ship features, but it is also creating a gap between product complexity and user understanding. Many SaaS products are becoming harder to adopt because feature velocity is outpacing user experience design, onboarding, and feedback loops. Product teams are building at a pace that would have been unthinkable a few years ago. Ideas turn into working features in hours. Prototypes no longer require weeks of coordination. Entire workflows can be generated, tested, and deployed in a single afternoon. That speed feels like progress and it often looks like progress too. But beneath that momentum, a gap is growing. Products are evolving faster than users can understand them. Features are being shipped faster than they are adopted. And in many cases, teams are solving problems without fully confirming that those problems exist in the first place. This is where many B2B SaaS companies are starting to lose ground. Not because they are moving too slowly, but because they are moving without enough clarity. Why AI Product Development Is Outpacing User Understanding AI-powered development has changed the constraints of product building. Engineering time used to be the bottleneck. Teams designed careful workflows to protect it. Low-fidelity mockups, staged prototyping, and structured validation cycles all existed to reduce the cost of getting something wrong. That constraint is gone. Today, a rough idea can become a functional prototype almost instantly. The barrier to building has collapsed, which means the cost of launching something is lower than ever. What hasn’t kept up is the speed of learning. User research, customer discovery, and real feedback loops still take time. Conversations still need context. Insights still require interpretation. While teams are building ten times faster, they are not learning ten times faster. That imbalance creates a dangerous pattern. Teams start relying on output as a proxy for progress. If something ships, it feels like momentum. If a feature exists, it feels like value has been created. In reality, many of those features go untouched. Why Shipping More Features Doesn’t Increase SaaS Adoption One of the clearest signals of this disconnect shows up in product analytics. Teams invest in building new capabilities, launch them, and then discover that only a small fraction of users ever engage with them. Sometimes that number is as low as four percent. So was anything actually achieved? The product may be more powerful, but power alone does not create value. If users cannot understand how to use a feature, or if it doesn’t align with how they think about their work, it might as well not exist. This is where fast building starts to work against the product. Instead of improving the experience, it adds complexity. Interfaces become harder to navigate. Workflows become less intuitive. The product begins to serve its most advanced users while leaving everyone else behind. Over time, that erodes adoption, retention, and expansion revenue. How Cognitive Load Impacts User Experience in SaaS Products Many teams approach user experience with a simple principle in mind. Reduce friction. Make everything faster. Remove as many steps as possible. That approach sounds right, but it often leads to the wrong outcomes. What users actually need is clarity. They need to understand what is happening, why it is happening, and what they should do next. When that clarity is missing, removing steps does not help. It can even make things worse. The real goal is to reduce cognitive load. Cognitive load reflects how much mental effort a user needs to interact with a product. When that effort is high, even simple tasks feel difficult. When it is low, complex workflows feel manageable. Sometimes reducing cognitive load requires adding friction. Asking a question before taking an action can prevent confusion. Giving users a moment to confirm a decision can improve confidence. Slowing things down in the right place can create a better overall experience. This requires a different mindset. Instead of optimizing for speed at every step, teams need to design for understanding. Most Products Are Built for the Wrong Users Another subtle issue is shaping many product decisions. Teams often build for the users who speak the loudest. These are usually power users. They are highly engaged, deeply familiar with the product, and quick to provide feedback. They request advanced features, more control, and greater flexibility. Listening to them feels productive. They are easy to reach and highly opinionated, but they rarely represent the majority of the user base. When product direction is driven primarily by these voices, the experience becomes skewed. New users struggle to get started. Occasional users feel lost. The product becomes increasingly specialized, even when the business depends on broader adoption. A better approach starts with recognizing different user stages. New users need guidance. They need clear entry points and simple workflows. As they gain experience, they can handle more complexity. Over time, they may become the power users who benefit from advanced capabilities. This progression does not happen automatically. It needs to be designed. Products that grow successfully guide users through that journey. They meet users where they are and help them build confidence step by step. Why SaaS Onboarding Is Critical for Product Adoption For many SaaS companies, onboarding is treated as a secondary concern. The focus stays on shipping features, improving performance, and expanding capabilities. That focus misses where most growth actually happens. Onboarding determines whether users understand the product. It shapes their first impression, their initial success, and their willingness to continue. A strong onboarding experience reduces confusion and builds momentum early. Without it, even a powerful product struggles. Users do not explore every feature. They do not read documentation in detail. They interact with what is in front of them and form quick judgments based on that experience. If the product feels overwhelming, they disengage. If it feels intuitive, they continue. This is why cognitive load matters so much at the beginning. The first interactions set the tone for everything that follows. How to Manage Rapid AI Development Without Creating Product Chaos The rise of rapid development has created a new kind of temptation. If something can be built quickly, it feels reasonable to try it. If it doesn’t work, it can always be replaced. That logic leads to constant iteration, but not necessarily meaningful progress. Without a clear understanding of the problem, iteration becomes guesswork. Teams build variations of the same idea without addressing the underlying need. Over time, this creates clutter rather than clarity. The discipline that used to come from technical constraints now has to be applied deliberately. That starts with problem definition. Before building anything, teams need confidence that the problem is real and worth solving. Once that is clear, rapid prototyping becomes a powerful tool. Ideas can be tested quickly, validated with users, and refined in short cycles. The key difference is intent. Building should serve learning. It should not replace it. Why User Feedback Is Still Essential in AI-Driven Product Development Access to user feedback has become more complicated in some ways. Traditional usability testing can be expensive. Recruiting participants takes effort. Scaling research across large audiences remains challenging. At the same time, new tools are making it easier to capture signals from different sources. Customer conversations, sales calls, and product usage data all contain valuable insights. AI can help process and organize that information at scale. Even with these advances, there is no substitute for direct interaction. Talking to users reveals context that data alone cannot capture. It exposes assumptions. It highlights unexpected behaviors. It shows how people actually use a product, not how teams think they use it. This includes users who never converted. Understanding why someone chose not to adopt the product can be as valuable as feedback from active customers. The challenge is not just collecting feedback. It is making sure the right voices are heard. That includes silent users, new users, and potential users who never engaged. Vision Still Has a Role There is an ongoing debate in product development. Some believe in strong vision, where leaders define the direction and build toward it. Others focus on continuous feedback, where products evolve based on user input. Both approaches have value. Short-term improvements often come from listening closely to users. Small adjustments, usability improvements, and incremental features benefit from direct feedback. Long-term progress requires a broader view. It involves looking beyond current workflows and imagining better ways to solve problems. Sometimes that means rethinking the entire system rather than optimizing individual steps. The most effective teams balance both. They use feedback to stay grounded in real user needs. At the same time, they maintain a clear direction that guides how the product evolves over time. What Product Leaders Should Do About AI-Driven Development Speed The current environment rewards speed, but it also punishes misalignment. Shipping quickly is no longer enough. Products need to be understood, adopted, and valued by a wide range of users. That requires a focus change. Product leaders need to think less about how fast their teams can build and more about how effectively their users can engage with what is built. They need to prioritize clarity over capability and understanding over output. This does not mean slowing down for the sake of it. It means being intentional about where speed is applied. Rapid prototyping, fast iteration, and continuous deployment are powerful tools. When they are combined with strong user insight and thoughtful design, they can accelerate real progress. Without that foundation, they create noise. The Gap That Defines the Next Phase of Growth The gap between building speed and user understanding is becoming one of the defining challenges for modern SaaS companies. Teams that close that gap will have a clear advantage. Their products will feel intuitive, even as they grow more powerful. Their users will adopt new features more easily. Their growth will come from deeper engagement rather than constant expansion. Teams that ignore it will continue to ship. They will continue to add features. But over time, they will struggle to convert that activity into meaningful results. The difference comes down to a simple principle. Building fast matters. Building something users can actually understand matters more. Feature velocity refers to how quickly a product team ships new features. While high feature velocity can signal innovation, it often leads to low adoption if users do not understand or need the new functionality. Why do users ignore new product features? Users ignore new features when they increase cognitive load, lack clear value, or are not integrated into existing workflows. Poor onboarding and misalignment with user needs are the most common causes. How does AI impact product development?
